Phlegmatic

fleg-MAT-ik · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Phlegmatic is unexcitable or unemotional, especially calm and unbothered under pressure.

While the rest of the office panicked over the server crash, the it director remained phlegmatic, calmly working through the checklist one item at a time.

Worked Example

The old sea captain stayed phlegmatic even as the storm tossed the ship violently, giving orders in the same flat, steady voice he always used.

Phlegmatic describes someone whose calm doesn't crack under pressure -- not because they don't notice the danger, but because their temperament simply doesn't excite easily.

How Phlegmatic Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

unflappable

unflappable: not easily upset or excited

even-tempered

even-tempered: having a steady, calm temperament

Antonyms

excitable

excitable: easily aroused to strong emotion

high-strung

high-strung: nervous and easily agitated

How Strong Is It? — relaxed → phlegmatic → impassive

relaxed vs. phlegmatic

relaxed vs. phlegmatic: Relaxed describes ordinary, everyday calm -- much milder than the deep, unshakable steadiness of phlegmatic.

impassive vs. phlegmatic

impassive vs. phlegmatic: Impassive describes a total absence of visible emotion, even more extreme than phlegmatic's steady calm.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — phlegm

root — phlegm: thick mucus; one of the four bodily 'humors' ancient doctors linked to a calm temperament (Greek phlegma)

suffix — -atic

suffix — -atic: having the qualities of (Greek/Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Phlegmatic comes from phlegm, one of the four 'humors' ancient physicians believed controlled personality. People thought to have too much phlegm were calm and unexcitable -- exactly what phlegmatic still describes today.

Word Choice

Phlegmatic describes a temperament, not a single reaction -- it's for people who are calm and hard to rattle as a general personality trait, not just calm in one moment.
